title: Lesson 7: Delivery Operations: Utilization, Capacity, and Margins
description: How a principal reads utilization, capacity, and margin as one system, names the binding constraint that sets throughput, and chooses an operating point instead of pushing any single number to its end.

questions.question: Why is 100 percent utilization a warning rather than a win?
options: It shows the practice is finally working at full efficiency.
It means the utilization denominator was defined too strictly.
It leaves no slack to absorb the unexpected, so every new demand becomes a queue.
It signals the practice has too many staff for its demand.
questions.explanation: Slack is the buffer that lets the system respond, and when nothing is free, an emergency, a failed review, or a new opportunity has nowhere to go, so the cost shows up later as rework and burnout.

questions.question: What sets the throughput of a delivery system?
options: The total number of people and agents it has.
The binding constraint, the slowest stage everything else queues behind.
The average utilization of the delivery team.
The size of the sales pipeline feeding it.
questions.explanation: Throughput is capped by the constraint, so adding capacity anywhere below it raises utilization without adding output, and the earliest honest signal is a growing queue in front of the constraint.

questions.question: Why does captured IP widen margin even when the price does not change?
options: Because it lowers the cost of delivery while the price stays set on the value of the outcome.
Because it lets the practice charge clients more for the same work.
Because it reduces the number of people needed to sell the work.
Because it allows utilization to run at 100 percent indefinitely.
questions.explanation: The price is anchored to the outcome, not the cost, so running delivery on captured method and tooling cuts cost per delivery and the difference becomes margin that funds the practice's future.
